name: K-factor
seoDesc: K-factor: work out bend allowance (BA) from the material thickness and the inside radius. A free construction calculator with the formula, units and a…
summary: The K-factor calculator turns the material thickness, the inside radius and the bend angle into bend allowance (BA). Think of it as a shortcut for a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. Change one value and the results step aside until you press Calculate again, which is what makes it easy to see how much the answer really depends on that one input.

sections.title: How does the K-factor calculator work?
sections.html:
The K-factor calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports bend allowance (BA) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the material thickness (T), the inside radius (Rᵢ) and the bend angle (θ).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the K-factor calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Bend allowance (BA)=(1 ÷ 180) × PI × bend angle (θ) × (inside radius (Rᵢ) + k-factor (K) × material thickness (T))
Location of neutral axis (t)=k-factor (K) × material thickness (T)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Material thickness (T) = 30 mm, Inside radius (Rᵢ) = 30 mm, Bend angle (θ) = 10 deg and K-factor (K) = 10. The calculator returns Bend allowance (BA) = 1.0052 mm and Location of neutral axis (t) = 300 mm.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Bend allowance (BA) = 1.0052 mm and Location of neutral axis (t) = 300 mm should be roughly the size you expected from Material thickness (T) = 30 mm and Inside radius (Rᵢ) = 30 mm.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in millimeters, and convertible to any of the 34 units on that chip.
  • Shown in millimeters, and convertible to any of the 34 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Angle, opening in degrees
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The K-factor calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the material thickness, the inside radius and the bend angle — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

faq.q: What does the K-factor calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns bend allowance (BA), derived from the material thickness, the inside radius and the bend angle. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the K-factor calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the material thickness, the inside radius and the bend angle, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter material thickness (T) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Material thickness (T) opens in millimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Bend allowance (BA) = 1.0052 mm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the K-factor calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
